title: You Know the Bible… But Why Do You Still Break People?
paragraphs:
You Know the Bible… But Why Do You Still Break People?
The terrifying truth about spiritual maturity without emotional transformation—and why Jesus refuses to leave you that way.
You can quote Scripture and still wound the people closest to you.
You can fast, pray, serve in ministry, lead worship… and still carry reactions that look nothing like Christ when someone challenges you, corrects you, or simply doesn’t meet your expectations.
And if that stung a little, stay here.

Because this is not an attack.
This is an exposure… the kind that leads to healing.
There is a dangerous illusion many believers live inside.

It sounds like this:
“If I know more about God, I must be growing in God.”
But Scripture never said knowledge alone transforms you.

Paul warned about this directly in 1 Corinthians 8:1:
“Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.”
The Greek word he used for “puffs up” is φυσιόω (physioō)—to inflate, to swell, to become proud. It paints a picture of something that looks bigger than it really is… something hollow inside.
So yes… you can grow in information and still be emotionally stunted.
You can look spiritually mature… and still respond like a wounded child.
And this is where the tension becomes uncomfortable.
Because Jesus never separated spiritual maturity from emotional transformation.
When He spoke about fruit in John 15, He wasn’t talking about how much Scripture you can memorize.
He was talking about what grows out of your life when pressure hits.

Galatians 5:22–23 says:
“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control…”
The original Greek word for patience is μακροθυμία (makrothymia)—long-suffering, the ability to endure difficult people without reacting in anger.
Self-control is ἐγκράτεια (enkrateia)—mastery over your internal world.
Not just your behavior in public… but your reactions in private.
So let’s ask the question honestly.
If someone criticizes you… what comes out?
If someone disappoints you… what rises up?
If someone wounds you… what do you release back into the world?
Because that… is your real level of maturity.
Not your Bible app streak.
Not your ministry title.
Not how many people think you’re “on fire for God.”
Your reactions reveal your formation.
And Jesus cares deeply about that.

In Luke 6:45, He said:
“Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.”
The Greek word for “abundance” is περίσσευμα (perisseuma)—overflow, surplus, what spills out when something is full.
Meaning… you don’t accidentally lash out.
You overflow what’s stored inside.
And this is where many believers wrestle silently.
Because they love God… but they haven’t allowed God into the places that shaped their emotional patterns.

The rejection.
The abandonment.
The betrayal.
The years of learning to survive instead of trust.
So they build spiritual habits… without surrendering emotional wounds.
They learn how to worship… but not how to process pain.
They learn how to preach truth… but not how to sit with their own brokenness.
And slowly… something dangerous forms.

A version of Christianity that looks strong… but reacts harshly.
A version of faith that speaks truth… but lacks tenderness.
A version of maturity that teaches others… but cannot be corrected.
And Jesus never modeled that.
Look at Him closely.
When He was betrayed, He didn’t explode.
When He was falsely accused, He didn’t defend His ego.
When He was crucified, He didn’t curse His enemies.

He said in Luke 23:34:
“Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”
The Aramaic root behind this expression carries the sense of releasing a debt… letting go of rightful offense.
That is not emotional suppression.
That is transformed emotion.
That is what it looks like when the Spirit of God doesn’t just inform your mind… but heals your heart.
And this is the invitation many are avoiding.
Because healing requires honesty.
And honesty feels like vulnerability.
And vulnerability feels like losing control.
But the truth?
You’re not losing control.
You’re finally surrendering it to the One who can actually transform you.

This is why David cried out in Psalm 51:10:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God…”
The Hebrew word for “create” is בָּרָא (bara)—the same word used in Genesis when God created the heavens and the earth.
David wasn’t asking for adjustment.
He was asking for recreation.
Because he understood something many still resist:
You don’t need behavior modification.
You need heart transformation.
And that includes your emotional life.

Your triggers.
Your tone.
Your reactions.
Your defensiveness.
Your silence when you should speak… and your harshness when you should listen.
Jesus is not just after your Sunday life.
He’s after your internal world.
And here’s the part many don’t want to hear…
If your spiritual growth is not making you more patient, more gentle, more forgiving, more self-controlled…
Then something is being built… but it’s not Christlikeness.
And deep down, you know it.
You’ve felt the tension.

The moments after you react and think,
“That wasn’t who I want to be.”
The silence after a harsh word.
The regret after an emotional outburst.
The distance it creates with people you actually love.
This is not condemnation.
This is invitation.
Because Jesus doesn’t expose to shame you.
He exposes to heal you.
And this is where everything shifts.
You don’t have to keep performing spirituality while hiding emotional immaturity.
You can bring both to the cross.
You can let Him rebuild you from the inside out.
You can become the kind of person whose presence feels like peace… not pressure.
Whose words heal… not cut.
Whose reactions reflect Christ… not past wounds.
But you have to be honest.
So be honest right here.
Let it be real.
Because someone else reading your comment might realize they’re not alone.
And if you feel something shifting inside you right now… don’t walk away from it.
Follow closely.
Stay near truth that refines you, not just comforts you.
Because this is deeper than information.
This is transformation.
And if you truly want to glorify God—not just in what you say, but in who you are becoming—then support what is feeding your spirit.
Because this journey is not about looking mature.
It’s about becoming like Him.
And He is not finished with you.
Not even close.

You don’t need to pretend you’re healed…
You just need to let Him touch the places you’ve been hiding.
